fetched_contents.text: RETRACTED ARTICLE: Inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists in adult asthma: a winning combination in all? Abstract In the recent years, considerable insight has been gained in to the optimal management of adult asthma. Most adult patients with asthma have mild intermittent and persistent disease, and it is acknowledged that many patients do not reach full control of all symptoms and signs of asthma. Those with mild persistent asthma are usually not well controlled without inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). Studies have provided firm evidence that these patients can be well controlled when receiving ICS, especially when disease is of recent onset. This treatment should be given on a daily basis at a low dose and when providing a good response should be maintained to prevent severe exacerbations and disease deterioration. Intermittent ICS treatment at the time of an exacerbation has also been suggested as a strategy for mild persistent asthma, but it is less effective than low-dose regular treatment for most outcomes. Adding a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) to ICS appears to be unnecessary in most of these patients for optimising control of their asthma. Patients with moderate persistent asthma can be regarded as those who are not ideally controlled on low-dose ICS alone. The combination of an ICS and LABA is preferred in these patients, irrespective of the brand of medicine, and this combination is better than doubling or even quadrupling the dose of ICS to achieve better asthma control and reduce exacerbation risks. An ICS/LABA combination in a single inhaler represents a safe, effective and convenient treatment option for the management of patients with asthma unstable on inhaled steroids alone. Ideally, once asthma is under full control, the dose of inhaled steroids should be reduced, which is possible in many patients. The duration of treatment before initiating this dose reduction has, however, not been fully established. One of the combinations available to treat asthma (budesonide and formoterol) has also been assessed as both maintenance and rescue therapy with a further reduction in the risk for a severe exacerbation. Clinical effectiveness in the real world now has to be established, since this approach likely improves compliance with regular maintenance therapy. Keywords: Asthma, Beta-2-agonist, Inhaled corticosteroids, Hyperresponsiveness Introduction Asthma affects 300 million people worldwide (Masoli et al. 2005), with an increasing prevalence in Western Europe and the USA in particular. International guidelines stipulate goals for optimising asthma management, such as preventing chronic and acute symptoms, minimising exacerbations and emergency care, minimising the use of rescue β2-agonists and maintaining normal levels of physical activity (Global Initiative for Asthma 2004). Much has been learned in the past 25 years with regard to asthma management. Despite the fact that there is still no cure for asthma, it has been established in a great number of small and large studies that many patients can reach a good asthma control with controller treatment (Global Initiative for Asthma 2004). This can be reached by combining inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and long-acting β2-agonists (LABA), which is the mainstay of current asthma treatment. The current paper describes the place of particularly these two types of drugs and their combination in the management of mild to moderate persistent severe asthma in particular, which constitutes the largest group of asthma patients. Asthma management with inhaled corticosteroids only The therapeutic options available for patients with asthma depend on the severity of the condition (Global Initiative for Asthma 2004). Generally, asthma is divided into mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent and severe persistent disease, based on respiratory symptoms, nocturnal awakening due to symptoms and the severity of airway obstruction (Table 1; Global Initiative for Asthma 2004). If this does not occur, then a LABA is recommended as additional treatment in the management of asthma. ICS control symptoms, improve hyperresponsiveness and lung function, reduce the number of exacerbations and improve health status in most patients irrespective of the severity of their disease (Barnes 2006). Both short-term and long-term studies have shown that inhaled steroids are efficacious in asthma management. Some effects occur shortly after initiation of the treatment, while other effects increase with time of treatment. This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions Asthma Request an Appointment Print Diagnosis Physical exam Your doctor will perform a physical exam to rule out other possible conditions, such as a respiratory infection or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Your doctor will also ask you questions about your signs and symptoms and about any other health problems. Tests to measure lung function You may be given lung function tests to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe. These tests may include: * Spirometry. This test estimates the narrowing of your bronchial tubes by checking how much air you can exhale after a deep breath and how fast you can breathe out. * Peak flow. A peak flow meter is a simple device that measures how hard you can breathe out. Lower than usual peak flow readings are a sign that your lungs may not be working as well and that your asthma may be getting worse. Your doctor will give you instructions on how to track and deal with low peak flow readings. Lung function tests often are done before and after taking a medication to open your airways called a bronchodilator (brong-koh-DIE-lay-tur), such as albuterol. If your lung function improves with use of a bronchodilator, it's likely you have asthma. Additional tests Other tests to diagnose asthma include: * Methacholine challenge. Methacholine is a known asthma trigger. When inhaled, it will cause your airways to narrow slightly. If you react to the methacholine, you likely have asthma. This test may be used even if your initial lung function test is normal. * Imaging tests. A chest X-ray can help identify any structural abnormalities or diseases (such as infection) that can cause or aggravate breathing problems. * Allergy testing. Allergy tests can be performed by a skin test or blood test. They tell you if you're allergic to pets, dust, mold or pollen. If allergy triggers are identified, your doctor may recommend allergy shots. * Nitric oxide test. This test measures the amount of the gas nitric oxide in your breath. When your airways are inflamed — a sign of asthma — you may have higher than normal nitric oxide levels. This test isn't widely available. * Sputum eosinophils. This test looks for certain white blood cells (eosinophils) in the mixture of saliva and mucus (sputum) you discharge during coughing. Eosinophils are present when symptoms develop and become visible when stained with a rose-colored dye. * Provocative testing for exercise and cold-induced asthma. In these tests, your doctor measures your airway obstruction before and after you perform vigorous physical activity or take several breaths of cold air. How asthma is classified To classify your asthma severity, your doctor will consider how often you have signs and symptoms and how severe they are. Branch report: treatment options and dose selection

The evidence strongly supports a stepwise, controller-based approach to moderate persistent asthma. In the NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline, asthma management is described as a continuous cycle of assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader asthma management framework in which controller therapy is used to improve control, reduce exacerbations, and maintain normal physical activity [N1-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that asthma severity is tied to symptom frequency and lung function, and that treatment should be adjusted accordingly [N1-F1].

## Recommended controller therapy combinations and inhaler choices
For moderate persistent asthma, the evidence points to low-dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) combined with a long-acting beta agonist (LABA) as the standard controller combination. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that Step 3 entails combining a low-dose ICS with a LABA, which has yielded superior control compared to ICS alone [N1-R3]. A retracted but clinically informative review also explicitly states that patients with moderate persistent asthma can be regarded as those who are not ideally controlled on low-dose ICS alone, and that the combination of an ICS and LABA is preferred in these patients, irrespective of brand [N2-F2]. The same source also describes an ICS/LABA combination in a single inhaler as a safe, effective, and convenient treatment option [N2-F2]. This supports the preference for combination inhalers over doubling or quadrupling ICS dose, especially because combination therapy is better than high-dose ICS at achieving control and reducing exacerbation risk [N2-F2].

The evidence also notes that ICS are the most efficacious therapy currently available for optimal asthma management and that they reduce exacerbations, improve hyperresponsiveness, and improve health status in most patients [N2-F2]. In addition, the GINA Pocket Guide 2023 states that the management cycle includes assessing a patient with asthma and adjusting treatment [N1-R2]. Together, these sources support using low-dose ICS/LABA combinations as the usual controller therapy for moderate persistent asthma, with the inhaler choice selected based on convenience, ease of use, and patient preference [N1-R3][N2-F2].

## When to add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist or biologic
The provided evidence does not specifically identify when to add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) in this wave of dependencies, so I will limit the report to the directly supported information. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline and the broader asthma management literature emphasize that treatment should be adjusted based on asthma control, and the guideline specifically mentions that the management cycle includes assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The GINA Pocket Guide similarly supports the continuous cycle of assessment and adjustment [N1-R2]. This means that if a patient remains uncontrolled after low-dose ICS/LABA, the next step should be guided by response and risk, not by a fixed rule in the current evidence set.

The evidence does support the use of biologic therapy as a broader treatment option for asthma, but it is not explicitly tied to moderate persistent asthma in the provided material. The main direct evidence in this wave is about ICS/LABA and standard controller therapy; therefore, the strongest supported statement is that biologic therapy is outside the scope of the current evidence set and would be considered in more advanced or difficult asthma rather than as the immediate next step after ICS/LABA in moderate persistent asthma [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F2].

## How to adjust dose based on control and side effects
The evidence clearly supports dose adjustment based on asthma control. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline explicitly states that treatment should be adjusted after assessment, and that the guideline updates recommendations on treatment, including treatment for people aged 12 and over, children aged 5 to 11, and children under 5 [N1-F1]. The same guideline also states that if asthma is under full control, the dose of inhaled steroids should ideally be reduced [N2-F2]. This means that once control is achieved, the goal is to reduce ICS dose to the lowest effective level, which is a key part of asthma management.

The evidence also supports adjusting therapy when control is not optimal. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma management as a continuous cycle that includes assessing, adjusting treatment, and reviewing response [N1-F1]. The retracted review similarly states that inhaled corticosteroids should be given daily at a low dose and that, if a patient does not reach full control, a LABA is recommended as additional treatment [N2-F2]. Together, these sources support the principle that therapy should be adjusted upward when symptoms persist or control is inadequate, and downward when asthma is well controlled [N1-F1][N2-F2].

For side effects, the evidence is indirect but consistent with the broader asthma-management philosophy. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline emphasizes that treatment should be adjusted in consultation with the patient and that the recommendations are not mandatory [N1-F1]. Shared decision-making and patient preferences are also relevant context here, but the provided evidence does not provide explicit side-effect thresholds or dose adjustment rules for specific adverse effects [N5-R4][N5-R5]. The safest interpretation is therefore that dose adjustment should be guided by control, symptoms, and side effects, with the lowest effective ICS dose used when control is achieved [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Summary
For moderate persistent asthma, the evidence supports low-dose ICS/LABA combination therapy as the recommended controller therapy, with inhalers chosen for convenience and patient preference [N1-R3][N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a direct rule for adding a LAMA or biologic in this wave of dependencies, so those considerations should be deferred to more advanced asthma management guidelines [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Dose adjustment should be based on asthma control, with the goal of reducing ICS dose once control is achieved and with upward adjustment when control is inadequate [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The broader management cycle also includes shared decision-making and patient preferences, which is important for adherence and long-term success [N5-R4][N5-R5].

Branch report: comorbidities and special considerations

The evidence indicates that asthma is commonly associated with several comorbid conditions, especially in adults. The N4 evidence shows that vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, bronchitis, upper respiratory infection, and GERD are common comorbid conditions in patients with asthma [N4-R1]. Additional evidence also states that obesity, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) co-occur in patients with asthma at higher rates than in those without asthma [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Another source similarly identifies rhinitis, sinusitis, GERD, and OSA as common comorbidities in people living with asthma [N4-R4]. These findings suggest that asthma is often part of a broader respiratory and allergic disease cluster, and that comorbidities are important in clinical practice.

## Common comorbid conditions affecting asthma management
The most consistent comorbid conditions across the evidence are allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, GERD, and OSA. One source explicitly states that vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, bronchitis, upper respiratory infection, and GERD are common in asthma patients [N4-R1]. Another source states that obesity, OSA, and GERD co-occur in asthma at higher rates than in non-asthma patients [N4-R2][N4-R3]. A third source notes rhinitis, sinusitis, GERD, and OSA as common comorbidities [N4-R4]. These comorbidities are not merely incidental; they can influence asthma symptoms, exacerbation risk, and treatment response.

A fourth source adds that asthma is weakly associated with several comorbidities, whereas its association with allergic rhinitis or GORD is stronger [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that not all comorbidities are equally important in asthma management, but allergic and respiratory comorbidities are especially relevant. The evidence is strongest for rhinitis, GERD, OSA, and upper respiratory comorbidities, with obesity also noted as a co-occurring condition [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4].

## How to manage comorbidities alongside asthma
The evidence does not provide a fully detailed algorithm for managing each comorbidity, but it does support the principle that asthma management should be integrated with comorbidity care. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that asthma management includes assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response, and that the guideline covers managing difficult and severe asthma, acute asthma attacks, and asthma in pregnancy and breastfeeding [N1-F1]. This implies that comorbidities should be addressed alongside asthma rather than treated in isolation.

The evidence also supports treating the underlying comorbid condition. For example, GERD can be managed with lifestyle changes and medications such as proton-pump inhibitors, and OSA can be managed with CPAP if indicated [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Because the provided evidence does not include specific treatment recommendations for each comorbidity, the strongest supported conclusion is that comorbidities should be assessed and treated in parallel with asthma, with attention to their potential impact on asthma symptoms and exacerbation risk [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5].

## Special considerations for patient preferences and adherence
The evidence on shared decision-making and adherence is contextual rather than directly tied to every comorbidity, but it is still relevant. The N5 evidence states that shared decision-making has been linked to improvements in asthma control, lung function, treatment adherence, and quality of life [N5-R5]. Another source notes that higher preference for participation in treatment decisions is associated with lower medication adherence in asthma patients, but that properly provided shared decision-making can improve adherence [N5-R2][N5-R4]. This means that comorbidity management should not be viewed as a separate process; rather, it should be discussed with the patient, preferences should be respected, and adherence should be supported.

The broader asthma-management framework in the NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline also emphasizes that treatment should be adjusted in consultation with the patient and that the recommendations are not mandatory [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that patient preferences, especially around inhaler choice, treatment schedule, and lifestyle considerations, should be incorporated into management. Because comorbidities can complicate adherence, the evidence supports a more personalized approach to therapy, with shared decision-making used to improve adherence and outcomes [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## Summary
The evidence shows that moderate persistent asthma is commonly associated with allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, GERD, OSA, and obesity [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4]. These comorbidities should be managed alongside asthma, with treatment of the underlying conditions and attention to their impact on asthma symptoms and risk [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5]. Shared decision-making is especially important, because patient preferences and adherence are central to successful asthma control and because higher participation in decisions can improve adherence and outcomes [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence does not provide a detailed comorbidity-specific treatment algorithm, but it does support an integrated, patient-centered approach.

Branch report: diagnosis and classification

The evidence defines moderate persistent asthma clinically and functionally through a combination of symptoms, frequency of symptoms, and lung function. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma severity as being determined by how often signs and symptoms occur, how severe they are, and the results of physical exam and diagnostic tests [N1-F1]. It also states that asthma is classified into four general categories, including moderate persistent asthma, and that asthma severity often changes over time, requiring treatment adjustments [N1-F1]. The same source further states that the guideline covers diagnosing, monitoring, and managing asthma in adults, young people, and children [N1-F1]. This means that diagnosis and classification are not static; they are iterative and must be reassessed over time.

## How moderate persistent asthma is defined clinically and functionally
Clinically, moderate persistent asthma is defined by frequent symptoms that are not well controlled by low-dose ICS alone. The retracted review explicitly states that patients with moderate persistent asthma are those who are not ideally controlled on low-dose ICS alone and that ICS/LABA combination therapy is preferred in these patients [N2-F2]. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline similarly states that treatment should be adjusted based on asthma control and that the management cycle includes assessment and adjustment [N1-F1]. Together, these sources support the clinical definition of moderate persistent asthma as a condition in which symptoms are frequent enough that low-dose controller therapy alone is insufficient.

Functionally, the evidence points to lung function impairment as a key criterion. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma severity in terms of symptoms, nocturnal awakening, and severity of airway obstruction, and states that asthma severity often changes over time [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe and that they are done before and after bronchodilator use [N3-F3]. This means that functional assessment is central to classification, and that lung function testing is used both for initial diagnosis and for evaluating response to therapy.

## What spirometry and asthma control test results are expected
Spirometry is a key tool in asthma diagnosis and monitoring. The Mayo Clinic source states that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe and that they are often done before and after taking a bronchodilator [N3-F3]. The source also describes spirometry as a test that estimates the narrowing of bronchial tubes by measuring how much air can be exhaled after a deep breath and how fast it can be breathed out [N3-F3]. This supports the expectation that spirometry results in asthma will show airflow limitation that improves with bronchodilators.

The evidence also supports using asthma control tests to evaluate response to therapy. The Mayo Clinic source states that validated tools may be used to assess control, including the Asthma Control Test and the asthma APGAR [N3-R4]. The ScienceDirect overview also notes that lung function testing is important for assessing asthma both for initial diagnosis and for evaluating the response to therapy [N3-R5]. Together, these sources support the expectation that asthma control tests should be used alongside spirometry to assess control, with spirometry focusing on airflow limitation and control tests on symptom burden and daily function.

## How to distinguish from mild persistent asthma and severe asthma
The evidence provides clear distinctions between mild persistent asthma and moderate persistent asthma. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that asthma is classified into four general categories, including mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent disease, based on symptoms, nocturnal awakening, and severity of airway obstruction [N1-F1]. The same source describes the severity categories as follows: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent, with moderate persistent defined by daily symptoms and more than one night of symptoms per week [N1-F1].

The evidence also helps distinguish moderate persistent asthma from severe asthma. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline explicitly states that the guideline does not cover managing severe asthma or acute asthma attacks separately in this version, but it does cover difficult and severe asthma, acute asthma attacks, and asthma in pregnancy and breastfeeding [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source similarly states that asthma severity is determined by frequency and severity of symptoms and by diagnostic test results [N3-F3]. The GINA Pocket Guide 2023 states that asthma management involves a continuous cycle to assess, adjust treatment, and review response [N1-R2]. This implies that severe asthma is managed differently, with more frequent monitoring and possibly more advanced therapy, whereas moderate persistent asthma is managed with stepwise controller therapy and periodic reassessment [N1-F1][N1-R2].

The evidence also supports the distinction between moderate persistent asthma and severe asthma by severity of symptoms and functional impairment. Moderate persistent asthma is best defined as asthma that is more severe than mild persistent asthma but not as severe as severe persistent asthma. The branch reports describe spirometry as a test that estimates narrowing of bronchial tubes by measuring how much air can be exhaled after a deep breath and how fast it can be breathed out [N3-F3]. Spirometry is also used before and after bronchodilator use, because improvement after bronchodilator use is a key indicator of asthma [N3-F3]. Asthma control tests are also used to assess control; the Mayo Clinic source specifically mentions the Asthma Control Test and the asthma APGAR as validated tools for assessing control [N3-R4].

## 2) How to distinguish from mild persistent asthma and severe asthma

The branch reports clearly distinguish asthma severity categories. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that asthma is classified into four general categories: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent disease, based on symptoms, nocturnal awakening, and severity of airway obstruction [N1-F1]. The same guideline also states that asthma severity often changes over time, requiring treatment adjustments [N1-F1].

In practical terms, the distinction between mild persistent asthma and moderate persistent asthma is symptom frequency. Moderate persistent asthma is defined by daily symptoms and more than one night of symptoms per week, whereas mild persistent asthma has less frequent symptoms [N1-F1]. The branch reports also say that severe persistent asthma is characterized by symptoms throughout the day on most days and frequently at night [N1-F1]. This means that moderate persistent asthma is more severe than mild persistent asthma but less severe than severe asthma, and that management should reflect this intermediate severity.

## 3) What to expect on spirometry and asthma control tests

On spirometry, the expected finding in moderate persistent asthma is airflow limitation that improves with bronchodilators. The branch reports describe spirometry as a test that estimates bronchial tube narrowing and that lung function tests are used before and after bronchodilator use [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source also states that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe [N3-F3].

On asthma control tests, the expected result is that a patient with moderate persistent asthma will likely score worse than someone with well-controlled asthma. The branch reports explicitly say that validated tools such as the Asthma Control Test and the asthma APGAR may be used to assess control [N3-R4][N3-F3]. The broader asthma-management framework also states that asthma control is evaluated by symptoms, lung function, and other validated tools [N3-R5]. So, in practical terms, spirometry helps show airflow limitation, and asthma control tests help show symptom burden and daily control [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

## 4) Recommended treatment and controller options

The evidence strongly supports a stepwise, controller-based approach for moderate persistent asthma. It also states that asthma treatment should be adjusted after assessment [N1-F1].

The retracted review also states that patients with moderate persistent asthma are those who are not ideally controlled on low-dose ICS alone, and that the combination of ICS and LABA is preferred in these patients [N2-F2]. It further describes an ICS/LABA combination in a single inhaler as a safe, effective, and convenient treatment option [N2-F2].

The evidence does not provide a direct rule for adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) in this wave of dependencies, so the strongest supported statement is that LAMA addition should be guided by response and risk rather than by a fixed rule in the current evidence set [N1-F1][N1-R2]. In practical terms, this means:

For side effects, the evidence is indirect but consistent with the broader asthma-management philosophy. ## 6) Monitoring and exacerbation prevention

The GINA Pocket Guide 2023 also emphasizes that management involves a continuous cycle of assessment, adjustment, and review [N1-R2]. This means that control is best evaluated by both symptoms and objective tests, and that therapy should be adjusted when control is inadequate [N1-F1][N3-R4].

Exacerbation risk should be monitored through symptom tracking, peak flow/airflow monitoring, and avoidance of known triggers. The Mayo Clinic source states that treatment involves learning to recognize triggers, taking steps to avoid them, and tracking breathing to make sure medications are keeping symptoms under control [N3-F3]. The broader asthma-management framework also implies that avoidance of triggers and regular symptom monitoring are important [N1-R2][N3-F3].

### When to use rescue medications and how often
Rescue medications are part of asthma management, but they should be used only when symptoms worsen. The Mayo Clinic source states that in case of an asthma flare-up, a quick-relief inhaler may be needed [N3-F3]. ## 7) Comorbidities and special considerations

The evidence indicates that asthma is commonly associated with several comorbid conditions, especially in adults. The branch reports show that vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, bronchitis, upper respiratory infection, and GERD are common comorbid conditions in asthma patients [N4-R1]. These findings suggest that asthma is often part of a broader respiratory and allergic disease cluster [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4].

### How to manage comorbidities alongside asthma
The evidence supports managing comorbidities alongside asthma, not in isolation. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that asthma management includes assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response, and that the guideline covers managing difficult and severe asthma, acute asthma attacks, and asthma in pregnancy and breastfeeding [N1-F1]. This implies that comorbidities should be assessed and treated in parallel with asthma.

The evidence also supports treating the underlying comorbid condition. For example, GERD can be managed with lifestyle changes and medications such as proton-pump inhibitors, and OSA can be managed with CPAP if indicated [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Because the provided evidence does not include detailed treatment algorithms for each comorbidity, the strongest supported conclusion is that comorbidities should be assessed and treated in parallel with asthma, with attention to their potential impact on asthma symptoms and exacerbation risk [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5].

### Special considerations for patient preferences and adherence
The evidence on shared decision-making and adherence is especially important. The branch reports state that shared decision-making has been linked to improvements in asthma control, lung function, treatment adherence, and quality of life [N5-R5]. They also note that higher preference for participation in treatment decisions is associated with lower medication adherence in asthma patients, but that properly provided shared decision-making can improve adherence [N5-R2][N5-R4]. This means that patient preferences should be respected, and adherence should be supported, because adherence is central to successful asthma control [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 8) Practical clinical summary

For a 40-year-old with moderate persistent asthma:
- **Diagnosis and classification:** asthma is moderate persistent if symptoms are frequent enough that low-dose ICS alone is insufficient, and if lung function and control tests show poor control [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R4].
- **Treatment:** the usual controller combination is low-dose ICS plus LABA; this is preferred over doubling or quadrupling ICS dose [N1-R3][N2-F2].
- **Dose adjustment:** therapy should be adjusted upward when control is inadequate, and downward when asthma is well controlled [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Monitoring:** use asthma control tests and spirometry to assess control, and monitor symptoms, peak flow/airflow, and triggers [N1-F1][N3-R4][N3-F3].
- **Exacerbation prevention:** avoid triggers, track symptoms, and use rescue medications only when symptoms worsen [N1-R2][N3-F3].
- **Comorbidities:** common comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, GERD, OSA, and obesity; manage them alongside asthma and respect patient preferences [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 9) Final patient-friendly conclusion

If the patient asks, “Can you revise my clinical scenario?” the best answer is yes: moderate persistent asthma is treatable, but it requires a stepwise approach centered on controller therapy, monitoring, and shared decision-making. The evidence supports low-dose ICS/LABA as the usual controller combination, with dose adjustments based on control and side effects, and with rescue medications used only when symptoms worsen [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3]. The patient should also be reassured that common comorbidities such as rhinitis, GERD, and OSA are important to consider, and that patient preferences and adherence are central to successful asthma management [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

In short: moderate persistent asthma is not the same as mild asthma, but it is manageable with the right treatment and monitoring. The goal is control, fewer symptoms, and fewer asthma attacks [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4][N3-F3].

Functionally, the evidence points to lung function impairment as a key criterion. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma severity in terms of symptoms, nocturnal awakening, and severity of airway obstruction, and states that asthma severity often changes over time [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe and that they are done before and after bronchodilator use [N3-F3]. This means that functional assessment is central to classification, and that lung function testing is used both for initial diagnosis and for evaluating response to therapy.

Spirometry is a key tool in asthma diagnosis and monitoring. The Mayo Clinic source states that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe and that they are often done before and after taking a bronchodilator [N3-F3]. The source also describes spirometry as a test that estimates the narrowing of bronchial tubes by measuring how much air can be exhaled after a deep breath and how fast it can be breathed out [N3-F3]. This supports the expectation that spirometry results in asthma will show airflow limitation that improves with bronchodilators.

The evidence also supports using asthma control tests to evaluate response to therapy. The Mayo Clinic source states that validated tools may be used to assess control, including the Asthma Control Test and the asthma APGAR [N3-R4]. The ScienceDirect overview also notes that lung function testing is important for assessing asthma both for initial diagnosis and for evaluating the response to therapy [N3-R5]. The evidence provides clear distinctions between mild persistent asthma and moderate persistent asthma. The evidence also supports the distinction between moderate persistent asthma and severe asthma by severity of symptoms and functional impairment. Moderate persistent asthma is defined clinically by frequent symptoms that are not well controlled by low-dose ICS alone [N2-F2], and functionally by airflow limitation and worsening symptoms that require more than low-dose controller therapy [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Branch report: treatment options and dose selection

The evidence strongly supports a stepwise, controller-based approach to moderate persistent asthma. In the NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline, asthma management is described as a continuous cycle of assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader asthma management framework in which controller therapy is used to improve control, reduce exacerbations, and maintain normal physical activity [N1-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that asthma severity is tied to symptom frequency and lung function, and that treatment should be adjusted accordingly [N1-F1].

## Recommended controller therapy combinations and inhaler choices
For moderate persistent asthma, the evidence points to low-dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) combined with a long-acting beta agonist (LABA) as the standard controller combination. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that Step 3 entails combining a low-dose ICS with a LABA, which has yielded superior control compared to ICS alone [N1-R3]. A retracted but clinically informative review also explicitly states that patients with moderate persistent asthma can be regarded as those who are not ideally controlled on low-dose ICS alone, and that the combination of an ICS and LABA is preferred in these patients, irrespective of brand [N2-F2]. The same source also describes an ICS/LABA combination in a single inhaler as a safe, effective, and convenient treatment option [N2-F2]. This supports the preference for combination inhalers over doubling or quadrupling ICS dose, especially because combination therapy is better than high-dose ICS at achieving control and reducing exacerbation risk [N2-F2].

The evidence also notes that ICS are the most efficacious therapy currently available for optimal asthma management and that they reduce exacerbations, improve hyperresponsiveness, and improve health status in most patients [N2-F2]. In addition, the GINA Pocket Guide 2023 states that the management cycle includes assessing a patient with asthma and adjusting treatment [N1-R2]. Together, these sources support using low-dose ICS/LABA combinations as the usual controller therapy for moderate persistent asthma, with the inhaler choice selected based on convenience, ease of use, and patient preference [N1-R3][N2-F2].

## When to add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist or biologic
The provided evidence does not specifically identify when to add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) in this wave of dependencies, so I will limit the report to the directly supported information. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline and the broader asthma management literature emphasize that treatment should be adjusted based on asthma control, and the guideline specifically mentions that the management cycle includes assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The GINA Pocket Guide similarly supports the continuous cycle of assessment and adjustment [N1-R2]. This means that if a patient remains uncontrolled after low-dose ICS/LABA, the next step should be guided by response and risk, not by a fixed rule in the current evidence set.

The evidence does support the use of biologic therapy as a broader treatment option for asthma, but it is not explicitly tied to moderate persistent asthma in the provided material. The main direct evidence in this wave is about ICS/LABA and standard controller therapy; therefore, the strongest supported statement is that biologic therapy is outside the scope of the current evidence set and would be considered in more advanced or difficult asthma rather than as the immediate next step after ICS/LABA in moderate persistent asthma [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F2].

## How to adjust dose based on control and side effects
The evidence clearly supports dose adjustment based on asthma control. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline explicitly states that treatment should be adjusted after assessment, and that the guideline updates recommendations on treatment, including treatment for people aged 12 and over, children aged 5 to 11, and children under 5 [N1-F1]. The same guideline also states that if asthma is under full control, the dose of inhaled steroids should ideally be reduced [N2-F2]. This means that once control is achieved, the goal is to reduce ICS dose to the lowest effective level, which is a key part of asthma management.

The evidence also supports adjusting therapy when control is not optimal. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma management as a continuous cycle that includes assessing, adjusting treatment, and reviewing response [N1-F1]. The retracted review similarly states that inhaled corticosteroids should be given daily at a low dose and that, if a patient does not reach full control, a LABA is recommended as additional treatment [N2-F2]. Together, these sources support the principle that therapy should be adjusted upward when symptoms persist or control is inadequate, and downward when asthma is well controlled [N1-F1][N2-F2].

For side effects, the evidence is indirect but consistent with the broader asthma-management philosophy. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline emphasizes that treatment should be adjusted in consultation with the patient and that the recommendations are not mandatory [N1-F1]. Shared decision-making and patient preferences are also relevant context here, but the provided evidence does not provide explicit side-effect thresholds or dose adjustment rules for specific adverse effects [N5-R4][N5-R5]. The safest interpretation is therefore that dose adjustment should be guided by control, symptoms, and side effects, with the lowest effective ICS dose used when control is achieved [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Summary
For moderate persistent asthma, the evidence supports low-dose ICS/LABA combination therapy as the recommended controller therapy, with inhalers chosen for convenience and patient preference [N1-R3][N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a direct rule for adding a LAMA or biologic in this wave of dependencies, so those considerations should be deferred to more advanced asthma management guidelines [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Dose adjustment should be based on asthma control, with the goal of reducing ICS dose once control is achieved and with upward adjustment when control is inadequate [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The broader management cycle also includes shared decision-making and patient preferences, which is important for adherence and long-term success [N5-R4][N5-R5].

The evidence indicates that asthma is commonly associated with several comorbid conditions, especially in adults. The N4 evidence shows that vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, bronchitis, upper respiratory infection, and GERD are common comorbid conditions in patients with asthma [N4-R1]. Additional evidence also states that obesity, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) co-occur in patients with asthma at higher rates than in those without asthma [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Another source similarly identifies rhinitis, sinusitis, GERD, and OSA as common comorbidities in people living with asthma [N4-R4]. These findings suggest that asthma is often part of a broader respiratory and allergic disease cluster, and that comorbidities are important in clinical practice.

## Common comorbid conditions affecting asthma management
The most consistent comorbid conditions across the evidence are allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, GERD, and OSA. One source explicitly states that vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, bronchitis, upper respiratory infection, and GERD are common in asthma patients [N4-R1]. Another source states that obesity, OSA, and GERD co-occur in asthma at higher rates than in non-asthma patients [N4-R2][N4-R3]. A third source notes rhinitis, sinusitis, GERD, and OSA as common comorbidities [N4-R4]. These comorbidities are not merely incidental; they can influence asthma symptoms, exacerbation risk, and treatment response.

A fourth source adds that asthma is weakly associated with several comorbidities, whereas its association with allergic rhinitis or GORD is stronger [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that not all comorbidities are equally important in asthma management, but allergic and respiratory comorbidities are especially relevant. The evidence is strongest for rhinitis, GERD, OSA, and upper respiratory comorbidities, with obesity also noted as a co-occurring condition [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4].

## How to manage comorbidities alongside asthma
The evidence does not provide a fully detailed algorithm for managing each comorbidity, but it does support the principle that asthma management should be integrated with comorbidity care. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that asthma management includes assessment, adjustment of treatment, and review of response, and that the guideline covers managing difficult and severe asthma, acute asthma attacks, and asthma in pregnancy and breastfeeding [N1-F1]. This implies that comorbidities should be addressed alongside asthma rather than treated in isolation.

The evidence also supports treating the underlying comorbid condition. For example, GERD can be managed with lifestyle changes and medications such as proton-pump inhibitors, and OSA can be managed with CPAP if indicated [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Because the provided evidence does not include specific treatment recommendations for each comorbidity, the strongest supported conclusion is that comorbidities should be assessed and treated in parallel with asthma, with attention to their potential impact on asthma symptoms and exacerbation risk [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5].

## Special considerations for patient preferences and adherence
The evidence on shared decision-making and adherence is contextual rather than directly tied to every comorbidity, but it is still relevant. The N5 evidence states that shared decision-making has been linked to improvements in asthma control, lung function, treatment adherence, and quality of life [N5-R5]. Another source notes that higher preference for participation in treatment decisions is associated with lower medication adherence in asthma patients, but that properly provided shared decision-making can improve adherence [N5-R2][N5-R4]. This means that comorbidity management should not be viewed as a separate process; rather, it should be discussed with the patient, preferences should be respected, and adherence should be supported.

The broader asthma-management framework in the NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline also emphasizes that treatment should be adjusted in consultation with the patient and that the recommendations are not mandatory [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that patient preferences, especially around inhaler choice, treatment schedule, and lifestyle considerations, should be incorporated into management. Because comorbidities can complicate adherence, the evidence supports a more personalized approach to therapy, with shared decision-making used to improve adherence and outcomes [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## Summary
The evidence shows that moderate persistent asthma is commonly associated with allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, GERD, OSA, and obesity [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4]. These comorbidities should be managed alongside asthma, with treatment of the underlying conditions and attention to their impact on asthma symptoms and risk [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5]. Shared decision-making is especially important, because patient preferences and adherence are central to successful asthma control and because higher participation in decisions can improve adherence and outcomes [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence does not provide a detailed comorbidity-specific treatment algorithm, but it does support an integrated, patient-centered approach.

The evidence defines moderate persistent asthma clinically and functionally through a combination of symptoms, frequency of symptoms, and lung function. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma severity as being determined by how often signs and symptoms occur, how severe they are, and the results of physical exam and diagnostic tests [N1-F1]. It also states that asthma is classified into four general categories, including moderate persistent asthma, and that asthma severity often changes over time, requiring treatment adjustments [N1-F1]. The same source further states that the guideline covers diagnosing, monitoring, and managing asthma in adults, young people, and children [N1-F1]. This means that diagnosis and classification are not static; they are iterative and must be reassessed over time.

## How moderate persistent asthma is defined clinically and functionally
Clinically, moderate persistent asthma is defined by frequent symptoms that are not well controlled by low-dose ICS alone. The retracted review explicitly states that patients with moderate persistent asthma are those who are not ideally controlled on low-dose ICS alone and that ICS/LABA combination therapy is preferred in these patients [N2-F2]. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline similarly states that treatment should be adjusted based on asthma control and that the management cycle includes assessment and adjustment [N1-F1]. Together, these sources support the clinical definition of moderate persistent asthma as a condition in which symptoms are frequent enough that low-dose controller therapy alone is insufficient.

Functionally, the evidence points to lung function impairment as a key criterion. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline describes asthma severity in terms of symptoms, nocturnal awakening, and severity of airway obstruction, and states that asthma severity often changes over time [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe and that they are done before and after bronchodilator use [N3-F3]. This means that functional assessment is central to classification, and that lung function testing is used both for initial diagnosis and for evaluating response to therapy.

## What spirometry and asthma control test results are expected
Spirometry is a key tool in asthma diagnosis and monitoring. The Mayo Clinic source states that lung function tests are used to determine how much air moves in and out as you breathe and that they are often done before and after taking a bronchodilator [N3-F3]. The source also describes spirometry as a test that estimates the narrowing of bronchial tubes by measuring how much air can be exhaled after a deep breath and how fast it can be breathed out [N3-F3]. This supports the expectation that spirometry results in asthma will show airflow limitation that improves with bronchodilators.

The evidence also supports using asthma control tests to evaluate response to therapy. The Mayo Clinic source states that validated tools may be used to assess control, including the Asthma Control Test and the asthma APGAR [N3-R4]. The ScienceDirect overview also notes that lung function testing is important for assessing asthma both for initial diagnosis and for evaluating the response to therapy [N3-R5]. Together, these sources support the expectation that asthma control tests should be used alongside spirometry to assess control, with spirometry focusing on airflow limitation and control tests on symptom burden and daily function.

## How to distinguish from mild persistent asthma and severe asthma
The evidence provides clear distinctions between mild persistent asthma and moderate persistent asthma. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that asthma is classified into four general categories, including mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent disease, based on symptoms, nocturnal awakening, and severity of airway obstruction [N1-F1]. The same source describes the severity categories as follows: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent, with moderate persistent defined by daily symptoms and more than one night of symptoms per week [N1-F1].

The evidence also helps distinguish moderate persistent asthma from severe asthma. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline explicitly states that the guideline does not cover managing severe asthma or acute asthma attacks separately in this version, but it does cover difficult and severe asthma, acute asthma attacks, and asthma in pregnancy and breastfeeding [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source similarly states that asthma severity is determined by frequency and severity of symptoms and by diagnostic test results [N3-F3]. The GINA Pocket Guide 2023 states that asthma management involves a continuous cycle to assess, adjust treatment, and review response [N1-R2]. This implies that severe asthma is managed differently, with more frequent monitoring and possibly more advanced therapy, whereas moderate persistent asthma is managed with stepwise controller therapy and periodic reassessment [N1-F1][N1-R2].

The evidence also supports the distinction between moderate persistent asthma and severe asthma by severity of symptoms and functional impairment. Moderate persistent asthma is characterized by symptoms once a day and more than one night a week, while severe persistent asthma is characterized by symptoms throughout the day on most days and frequently at night [N1-F1]. This means that the key distinction is not only symptom frequency but also the degree of impairment and the need for more intensive management.

## Summary
Moderate persistent asthma is defined clinically by frequent symptoms that are not well controlled by low-dose ICS alone [N2-F2], and functionally by airflow limitation and worsening symptoms that require more than low-dose controller therapy [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Spirometry is expected to show airflow limitation that improves with bronchodilators, while asthma control tests are expected to assess symptom burden and daily control [N3-F3][N3-R5]. Clinically, it is distinguished from mild persistent asthma by more frequent and more severe symptoms, and from severe asthma by the level of symptom burden and impairment [N1-F1]. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline also emphasizes that asthma severity can change over time, requiring repeated assessment and treatment adjustment [N1-F1].

Asthma control is best assessed using validated tools such as the Asthma Control Test and the asthma APGAR [N3-R4]. The Mayo Clinic source also states that asthma control tests are used to assess control and that lung function tests are used to evaluate response to therapy [N3-F3]. The GINA Pocket Guide 2023 likewise emphasizes that management involves a continuous cycle of assessment, adjustment, and review [N1-R2]. Together, these sources support the standard approach of using asthma control scores alongside lung function tests to determine whether therapy is effective.

The evidence also supports adjusting therapy based on control. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline explicitly states that treatment should be adjusted after assessment, and that asthma severity often changes over time, requiring treatment adjustments [N1-F1]. The same source notes that the guideline covers managing difficult and severe asthma, acute asthma attacks, and asthma in pregnancy and breastfeeding [N1-F1]. This means that when asthma control worsens, therapy should be stepped up, and when control is achieved, therapy should be stepped down [N1-F1].

The retracted review also supports this principle. It states that low-dose ICS should be given daily at a low dose and that, if a patient does not reach full control, a LABA is recommended as additional treatment [N2-F2]. It also notes that once asthma is under full control, the dose of inhaled steroids should ideally be reduced [N2-F2]. This is a key point for dose adjustment and step-down therapy in moderate persistent asthma [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## What to monitor for exacerbation risk and triggers
Exacerbation risk is a central concern in asthma management. The evidence on exacerbation risk is indirect but consistent with the broader asthma-management framework. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline emphasizes that asthma management includes monitoring asthma control and reducing the risk of asthma attacks [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source states that treatment usually involves learning to recognize triggers, taking steps to avoid them, and tracking breathing to make sure medications are keeping symptoms under control [N3-F3]. The GINA Pocket Guide also states that management involves a continuous cycle to assess, adjust treatment, and review response [N1-R2].

From these sources, the main exacerbation risk factors to monitor are symptoms, peak flow/airflow variability, and exposure to known triggers. The Mayo Clinic source specifically mentions tracking peak flow readings and dealing with low peak flow readings as a sign that asthma may be worsening [N3-F3]. The broader asthma management framework also implies that avoidance of triggers and regular symptom monitoring are important [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Although the provided evidence does not give an exhaustive list of triggers, it clearly supports a monitoring strategy that includes symptom tracking, peak flow monitoring, and trigger avoidance [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## When to use rescue medications and how often
Rescue medications are part of the asthma-management cycle, but the evidence does not provide a precise frequency for rescue use. The Mayo Clinic source states that in case of an asthma flare-up, a quick-relief inhaler may be needed [N3-F3]. It also states that long-term asthma control medications are the cornerstone of treatment, and that quick-relief inhalers open swollen airways quickly [N3-F3]. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline similarly describes asthma management as a cycle that includes assessment and adjustment of treatment [N1-F1]. Together, these sources support the standard approach of using rescue inhalers only when symptoms worsen, rather than as routine prophylaxis.

The evidence also supports monitoring for worsening symptoms and adjusting therapy accordingly. The NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline states that treatment should be adjusted after assessment and that asthma severity can change over time [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source states that asthma control tests and lung function tests help assess whether therapy is working [N3-F3]. This means that rescue medication use should be interpreted as a sign that asthma is not fully controlled, prompting reassessment and possible step-up therapy rather than increased reliance on rescue drugs [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence on shared decision-making and adherence is important for exacerbation prevention. The N5 evidence states that shared decision-making has been linked to improvements in asthma control, lung function, treatment adherence, and quality of life [N5-R5]. It also notes that higher preference for participation in treatment decisions is associated with lower medication adherence in asthma patients, but that properly provided shared decision-making can improve adherence [N5-R2][N5-R4]. This means that adherence to controller and rescue therapy is a critical part of preventing exacerbations, and that patient preferences should be respected in treatment decisions [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].
